locations.line: Bunbury is supplied from our Western Australian stock at a Fremantle depot, trucked down the Kwinana Freeway and the Forrest Highway. The drive is easy. The local questions are about winter-wet ground, dairy and farm access inland, and industrial sites around the port and Kemerton.
locations.opener: The South West's biggest town, answered plainly.
locations.usesHead: What people around Bunbury use them for
uses: Bunbury's port, the alumina and mineral sands operations in the district, and the Kemerton industrial area up the road keep a steady stream of contractors busy, and contractors want secure storage they can shift when the job moves. A cargo-worthy container, bought or hired, does exactly that.

Around town and out through Australind, Eaton, Dalyellup and Gelorup it is household and trade storage — renovation overflow, a tradie's materials, the contents of a house between moves. On the farms toward Harvey, Brunswick Junction, Dardanup and Boyanup it is fertiliser, fencing materials, calf-rearing gear and spare parts that should not live in an open shed.
locations.stockHead: Where it comes from — no Bunbury yard
stock: There is no yard of ours in Bunbury and no staff in the South West. We hold our WA stock at a third-party depot in Fremantle, and your container is loaded there and trucked down.

To see the unit before it arrives, we can arrange an inspection at the Fremantle depot, or send photographs of that exact container on request, before delivery. Pricing, questions and booking all happen over the phone.
locations.checksIntro: Bunbury deliveries are usually uncomplicated, but a handful of local conditions trip people up. Look at these first.

checks.h: Will the spot be under water in July?
checks.p: The South West gets more winter rain than Perth, and the low ground around the Leschenault Estuary, the Collie and Preston river flats and parts of Australind stays wet for long stretches. A container parked in a damp hollow rusts from the base up, and water that pools around it finds its way in at the door seals. Pick the highest point you have.

checks.h: Will the farm track hold up?
checks.p: The dairy and beef country inland from Bunbury is heavier soil than the coastal sand. After rain the paddocks, and some farm tracks, will not carry a loaded truck. If the ground is soaked, we would rather move the date than leave ruts across your paddock.

checks.h: Delivering into Kemerton or the port area?
checks.p: Industrial sites have gate procedures, inductions and set delivery hours. Send us the requirements and a contact name with the order so the truck is not held up at the gate.

checks.h: How close are the power lines?
checks.p: Older streets in Bunbury, South Bunbury and Carey Park carry overhead power along the front of the block. A tilt-tray raises its bed high at the back. If lines cross your driveway or run near the drop spot, tell us — it can change which truck is sent.

checks.h: Old trees over the driveway?
checks.p: Peppermints, tuarts and big street trees are part of the town's character, and they hang over driveways. Walk the route in and look up. A low limb that a car passes under easily can stop a tray.

checks.h: What is going inside, and does it need to stay bone dry?
checks.p: For anything that must stay dry through a South West winter, buy a grade sold wind and watertight — cargo-worthy or new — and fit vents. A closed box goes through a lot of mild-day, cold-night cycles here, and condensation drips off the roof onto whatever sits underneath.

sections.h: Winter on the coast and a steel box
p: Winter in Bunbury is cool and wet, with fronts rolling in off the Indian Ocean one after another. The container itself copes fine. What causes trouble is standing water around its base and moisture sealed up inside it.

Put it on pads or sleepers so water can run underneath rather than pond against it, keep gutters and downpipes from dumping onto the spot, and give the inside some airflow. Pallets under stored goods keep them off the floor if condensation does run down the walls.

sections.h: Sand on the coast, clay further in
p: Along the coast from Dalyellup up to Binningup the ground is mostly sand, often with limestone under it. It drains well and makes firm footing once compacted. Head inland past the highway toward Dardanup, Brunswick and Harvey and the soil gets heavier, holding water through winter and baking hard in summer.

On heavier ground, level the container on solid pads rather than straight onto the dirt, because clay that swells and shrinks with the seasons moves the corners unevenly. Doors that bind in winter and swing freely in summer tell you one corner needs packing.

sections.h: Inland: Ferguson Valley, Donnybrook and Collie
p: Head inland from Dardanup and the country climbs into the Ferguson Valley, then on to the orchards around Donnybrook and the jarrah forest around Collie. These are hillier, more timbered deliveries than anything on the coastal plain: narrow sealed roads, steep gravel driveways and trees crowding the approach.

Orchards use containers for packing supplies, ladders and tools between seasons. Collie's mine and power station contractors, and the town's households, use them the same way people do everywhere. Whichever it is, send photos of the last stretch of driveway and the spot itself. In the hills, the final few hundred metres decide the truck far more than the distance from Fremantle does.

locations.accessHead: What the truck needs at your place
access: A tilt-tray handles most Bunbury homes for a 10ft or 20ft: straight approach, firm footing, room overhead. Newer estates in Dalyellup, Millbridge and Treendale often have narrow frontages and side fences close to the house, which pushes the job toward a side loader.
A 40ft is usually a farm or industrial delivery. It needs a long clear run, plenty of room to place it, and ground under the truck that is solid the whole way.
locations.freightHead: What getting it down south costs
freight: The delivery is quoted with the container, for your address. It depends on the run down from Fremantle and what your site needs from the truck. There is no single Bunbury figure — the quote gives you the real one.
locations.faqHead: Questions from Bunbury and the South West

faqs.q: Is there a yard near Bunbury where I can see stock?
faqs.a: No. We do not have premises in the South West. Our WA stock is held at a Fremantle depot run by a third party; you can arrange to inspect a unit there, or ask us to send photos before delivery.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to a dairy farm near Harvey?
faqs.a: Yes. Give us the gate width, what the track is like and whether there is room to turn. In winter we will ask whether the ground is firm enough, because a bogged truck on a wet paddock ruins everyone's day.

faqs.q: Do containers sweat inside?
faqs.a: They can, especially through a South West winter. Mild days and cold nights make moisture condense under the roof. Vents, airflow, and not storing damp goods inside are the answer.

faqs.q: Do I need approval in Bunbury?
faqs.a: It depends on the council — the City of Bunbury, the Shire of Harvey, the Shire of Dardanup and the Shire of Capel each cover part of greater Bunbury — and on how long the container stays and what it is for. Check with yours before delivery.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to Collie?
faqs.a: Yes. Collie is inland on the Coalfields Highway. Tell us the address and the access and we will price it the same way as anywhere else.

faqs.q: Is as-is stock fine for a farm shed?
faqs.a: As-is units are cheaper and are not sold watertight. Under an existing roof, or for gear that does not mind some weather, they are fine. For fertiliser, feed or anything that has to stay dry, pay for cargo-worthy.

locations.askSub: Give us the town or suburb, a photo of the access and what is going inside, and we will price the container with delivery from Fremantle.

locations.line: Busselton, Dunsborough and Margaret River are supplied from our WA container stock at a Fremantle depot, trucked south down the Forrest and Bussell highways. Getting the container there is not the hard bit. Long gravel driveways, tall karri and marri, low wetland ground near the bay and holiday-town rules are what need checking.
locations.opener: The Capes, without the brochure talk.
locations.usesHead: What goes in a container down here
uses: The region lives on wine, tourism and building. Vineyards and wineries use containers for bottling supplies, cellar-door dry goods, bird netting, tools, and the vintage gear that sits idle most of the year. Builders — and there are plenty working between Busselton and Margaret River — use them as lockable site stores on house jobs.

Owners of holiday houses in Dunsborough, Yallingup and Gracetown use them to lock away linen, surfboards, kayaks and gear between stays. Farmers on the cattle and dairy country around Vasse, Metricup and Cowaramup keep feed and fencing gear in them. And people moving to the region full-time use one to hold the contents of the old house while the new one is finished.
locations.stockHead: Where your container is coming from
stock: We have no depot, office or staff in the South West. Our Western Australian stock is held at a third-party container depot in Fremantle, and orders for the Capes are loaded there and trucked down.
An inspection at the Fremantle depot can be arranged if you would like to see the unit. If you would rather not make the trip, we will send photos of the actual container on request, before delivery.
locations.checksIntro: The Capes have some of the most varied delivery sites in WA — beach sand, bay-side flats and forest blocks along one short stretch of coast. Here is what to check.

checks.h: Forest block with big trees?
checks.p: Karri, marri and jarrah around Margaret River, Cowaramup and Witchcliffe grow tall and spread wide. A tilt-tray needs clear air above it as the bed lifts. Where the canopy closes over the driveway, a crane truck placing from a clearing — or a different spot — is often the answer.

checks.h: How long and how steep is the driveway?
checks.p: Rural blocks through the Capes often have long gravel driveways with dips, creek crossings and sharp bends. A loaded truck needs firm footing the whole way and somewhere to turn. Photos taken along the driveway, not only at the house, tell us the most.

checks.h: Is the ground near Busselton low and wet?
checks.p: The land behind the bay around Busselton, Vasse and Wonnerup is flat and low, with wetlands and drains that fill through winter. Pick a raised, firm spot and set the container on pads. Water pooling at the door seals gets in; a container does not keep out rising water.

checks.h: Bushfire: what surrounds the container?
checks.p: Much of the Capes is bushfire-prone country. A container is not a fire shelter and will not protect what is inside from fire. Keep grass, leaf litter and firewood well clear of it, think hard before storing fuel in it, and site it where it will not block your own access or a firebreak.

checks.h: Holiday rental, strata or estate rules?
checks.p: If the property is a short-stay rental, or part of a strata or estate scheme, check the by-laws and the council's rules before a container arrives. What is fine on a farm is not always fine beside a holiday house.

checks.h: Which council is yours?
checks.p: Busselton, Dunsborough and Yallingup sit in the City of Busselton. Margaret River, Cowaramup and Augusta are in the Shire of Augusta-Margaret River. Ask the right one about approvals and firebreak requirements before delivery.

sections.h: Vineyards, bush blocks and long driveways
p: The country between Cowaramup and Witchcliffe is gravelly loam over granite, rolling and timbered. It carries a truck well in summer and can turn greasy after winter rain, particularly on the clay patches at the bottom of a slope. Tell us if your driveway runs downhill to the house, because the truck has to climb back out.

On a vineyard or winery, think about where the container will earn its keep at vintage: close enough to the shed to save walking, clear of where bins and machinery move, and somewhere a truck can reach again if you ever want it shifted.

Right along Geographe Bay, from Busselton through Abbey and Broadwater to Dunsborough, blocks mostly sit on sand close to sea level. Firm, compacted sand is fine under a container. Soft, freshly dug sand is not.

Living by the water means salt on the steel. Look after the paint, wash it down now and then, and keep the base clear of sand drifts. A new or cargo-worthy unit — the grades sold wind and watertight — is worth the extra if the container is staying near the beach for years.

sections.h: Building down south: site boxes and staged moves
p: A lot of containers in the Capes arrive at the start of a house build and leave at the end of it. If that is you, talk to your builder before you order. They will know where the slab, the scaffold, the skip and the concrete truck need to go, and a container dropped in the wrong corner on day one gets in the way for months.

If you are moving into the region and the new house is not finished, a container on the block — or at a relative's place — can hold the contents of the old one. Pack it tight, load the heaviest things low and towards the front wall, and keep a clear aisle so you can reach the box of paperwork you will inevitably need. Hire makes sense when you know it is temporary; buying makes sense when it will end up as the garden shed.

access: On a town lot in Busselton or Dunsborough, a tilt-tray usually does the job if there is a straight run in and clear air overhead. Tight holiday-house blocks with no side access may need a side loader or crane.

On a rural block, the truck's path from the road to the spot matters most: firm ground, width through the gates, clearance under branches, and somewhere to turn around. A 40ft needs a lot of room and is mostly a farm or vineyard job.
locations.freightHead: The cost of getting it to the Capes
freight: Delivery is worked out with the container for your particular property. A town lot in Busselton and a forest block past Margaret River are priced differently, so there is no set figure here — the quote gives you the real one.
locations.faqHead: Common questions from Busselton to Margaret River

faqs.q: Do you have a yard in Busselton or Margaret River?
faqs.a: No. We have no local premises in the South West. WA stock is held at a third-party depot in Fremantle — inspection there can be arranged, or we send photos of the exact unit before delivery.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to a vineyard?
faqs.a: Yes. Tell us where on the property it is going, what the tracks are like, and whether trellis rows, netting or overhead lines are in the way. Photos of the route in help us send the right truck.

faqs.q: Is a container a safe place during a bushfire?
faqs.a: No. Do not shelter in one and do not rely on it to protect contents from fire. Follow the fire authorities' advice for your area, and keep the ground around the container clear of fuel.

faqs.q: Can I keep one at a holiday house?
faqs.a: Often, but check with the City of Busselton or the Shire of Augusta-Margaret River first, and with the strata or estate if there is one. The rules for a residential lot are not always the same as for a farm.

faqs.q: Will it get mouldy inside?
faqs.a: It can if damp things are locked in without airflow. Fit vents, dry towels, wetsuits and linen before they go in, and choose a cargo-worthy or new unit to keep the rain out.

faqs.q: What if the driveway is too steep?
faqs.a: Then we tell you before booking. Sometimes the answer is a different spot nearer the road, sometimes a crane truck. Far better to hear it on the phone than have the driver turn around.

locations.askHead: Tell us about the Capes property
locations.askSub: Send the address, photos of the driveway and the spot, and what is going inside, and we will price it with delivery from Fremantle.

locations.line: Albany is a long way from the Fremantle depot where our Western Australian stock is held, and we will not pretend otherwise. Because of that, getting the size, the grade and the access right before the truck leaves matters more here than almost anywhere else in WA.
locations.opener: A long way from Fremantle, so get it right first time.
locations.usesHead: What Albany and the Great Southern use them for
uses: Albany's port moves grain and woodchips, and the farms behind it run sheep, cattle and crops over a wide stretch of country toward Mount Barker, Kendenup and the Porongurups. On those farms a container is a dry, lockable store for seed, fertiliser, shearing gear, fencing materials and workshop tools.

In and around town, from Middleton Beach and Spencer Park out to Little Grove, Lower King and Kalgan, it is household storage, boat and fishing gear, and builders' site boxes. Plenty of people retiring to the south coast use one to hold what did not fit in the smaller house.
locations.stockHead: No yard in Albany — the honest version
stock: We have no yard, office or staff in Albany or anywhere in the Great Southern. Our WA stock sits at a third-party container depot in Fremantle, and an Albany order makes the full trip south by road.

That distance is exactly why we would rather you saw the unit first. You can inspect it at the Fremantle depot by arrangement if you happen to be in Perth, or we will send photos of the specific container on request, before delivery. Either way, you should know what is coming before it comes all that way.
locations.checksIntro: With a long haul in the mix, the aim is one trip that works. Go through these before you order.

checks.h: Have you actually measured the spot?
checks.p: Measure the space, not the gap you think you have. Add room to swing the doors fully and to walk around the container. Swapping a container in Albany for a bigger one is a long round trip, so check twice.

checks.h: Is there granite under the surface?
checks.p: Albany sits among granite — Mount Clarence, Mount Melville, the coast out toward Torndirrup — and many blocks have rock at or just under the surface. That makes for excellent footing and awkward levelling. Plan to build up the low corners with solid packing rather than dig.

checks.h: Is the drop spot on a slope?
checks.p: Many Albany blocks fall toward the harbour or the Sound. A tilt-tray needs a reasonably level area to set a container down without it skewing off the bed. Steep sites often become crane jobs.

checks.h: Is the grade right for the rain?
checks.p: Albany gets plenty of rain and drizzle through the cooler months and a lot of grey, damp days. For anything that has to stay dry, buy cargo-worthy or new single-trip — the grades sold wind and watertight. As-is is not sold watertight and is a poor fit for an exposed spot on the south coast.

checks.h: Will the farm track take a loaded truck after rain?
checks.p: Great Southern farm tracks over clay and gravel go soft through winter. Tell us about the track honestly, and be ready to shift the date if it has been wet.

checks.h: Could the order be combined?
checks.p: If a neighbour, a relative or another part of your business also needs a container, say so. Two units travelling together on a long run is always worth asking about.

sections.h: Damp air, condensation and a steel roof
p: The south coast is mild but moist. Cool nights, sea air and long runs of damp weather mean a sealed steel box collects condensation under its roof and drips it onto whatever is stored below. It is the commonest complaint about containers in cool, wet places, and it is fixable.

Fit vents at both ends so air can move. Keep stored goods off the floor on pallets and away from the walls. Do not lock away wet gear. For a workshop or anything you will spend time in, line and insulate the roof — that stops most of the drip.

sections.h: Salt wind off the Southern Ocean
p: Southerly weather comes straight off the Southern Ocean, and anything near Middleton Beach, Emu Point or the Torndirrup side cops salt spray on the wind. Watch the paint, especially at the bottom rails, the door gear and anywhere water sits.

Point the doors away from the prevailing weather where the block allows, so rain is not driven against the seals all winter. A container sitting on pads, with air moving under it, lasts far longer here than one sitting in wet grass.

sections.h: West to Denmark and Walpole: forest country
p: West of Albany toward Denmark, Nornalup and Walpole the country turns to karri and tingle forest, with high rainfall, narrow winding roads and steep driveways cut into the hillside. A block that is easy in a ute can be a real problem for a truck carrying a container.

If you are out that way, send photos of the driveway from the road all the way to the spot, and of anything overhead along it. Tell us whether the surface is gravel or bitumen and how it behaves after rain. Some of these properties are best served by a spot near the front gate rather than up at the house, and it is far better to agree that on the phone than to find it out on the day.

access: On a standard suburban block with a straight driveway, a tilt-tray places a 10ft or 20ft easily. Older, steeper blocks around the town centre and the slopes of Mount Clarence may need a crane truck parked on the street.

Farm deliveries need firm, wide access and somewhere to turn. A 40ft suits most farms if the track and gateways allow it — but tell us about every gate, grid and culvert between the road and the spot.
locations.freightHead: Why there is no delivery figure on this page
freight: Albany is a long run from Fremantle, and the cost of getting a container here depends on the trip, the truck your site needs and whether it can travel with another load. We price it with the container for your address and give you one number. A figure published here would only be a guess.
locations.faqHead: What Albany callers want to know

faqs.q: Why don't you have a yard in Albany?
faqs.a: Because we are not a local business, and we would rather say so than dress it up. WA orders are supplied from stock at a Fremantle depot operated by a third party. You can inspect there by arrangement, or have photographs sent before delivery.

faqs.q: Is it worth bringing a container all the way to Albany?
faqs.a: If you need secure, dry storage and there is nothing suitable closer, yes. Get the size and grade right and sort out the access first, so it is a single trip. We will tell you honestly if something about the job does not add up.

faqs.q: Can I stop condensation inside?
faqs.a: You can cut it right back. Vents at both ends, goods off the floor and away from the walls, nothing put away wet, and an insulated roof if you are using it as a workspace.

faqs.q: Do I need approval from the City of Albany?
faqs.a: It depends on your zoning, how long it will stay and what it is for, and rural and residential lots are treated differently. Check with the City of Albany — or the Shire of Plantagenet or the Shire of Denmark if you are on their side — before you order.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to Denmark or Mount Barker?
faqs.a: Yes. Give us the address and the access details and we will price it with the container.

faqs.q: When will it arrive?
faqs.a: We will tell you honestly what is achievable when you ring, and confirm the date when you order. If you have a hard deadline, raise it at the very start.

locations.askHead: Tell us about the Great Southern job
locations.askSub: Give us the town, the access and what is going in it. With the distance involved, a photo of the spot helps us get it right in one trip.

locations.line: Geraldton orders come up the Brand Highway from container stock held at a Fremantle depot. The Mid West has its own set of questions — the wind, blowing sand, salt, and big cropping properties inland — and this page answers them plainly.
uses: The port, the grain handling and the mining supply trade keep Geraldton busy, and the Narngulu industrial estate and the light industrial areas around town use containers as secure stores, parts rooms and site offices. Contractors working inland take hire units out to the job and bring them back when it wraps up.

On the farms — the Chapman Valley, the Greenough flats, out toward Mullewa and up to Northampton — a container keeps seed, fertiliser, tools and machinery parts dry and locked up through seeding and harvest. In town, from Beachlands and Tarcoola Beach to Waggrakine and Drummond Cove, it is household storage, boat and cray gear, and room to breathe during a move.
locations.stockHead: No Geraldton yard, and what that means
stock: We are not based in Geraldton and do not run a yard in the Mid West. WA stock is held at a third-party depot in Fremantle, and a Geraldton container is trucked north from there.

To see the unit, arrange an inspection at the Fremantle depot, or ask for photos of that specific container, which we send on request before delivery. It is a long enough trip that it pays to know exactly what is coming.
locations.checksIntro: Most of what goes wrong with a Mid West container is the weather after it arrives, not the delivery itself. Check these.

checks.h: Which way is the wind coming from?
checks.p: Geraldton is famously windy, with strong southerlies through summer. A door that opens into that wind is dangerous. Face the doors north, or at least out of the southerly, and fit something solid to hold them open.

checks.h: Will sand bank up against it?
checks.p: Blowing sand piles up against anything that stops it. A container with a drift along one side holds moisture there and rusts at the base. Choose a spot with some shelter, or plan to clear it regularly.

checks.h: What about tying it down?
checks.p: In strong-wind country people often ask about tie-down. We do not supply wind ratings or promise any particular result. If the container is staying, ask the City of Greater Geraldton or an engineer what is expected for your site. The Mid West remembers what Cyclone Seroja did to Kalbarri and Northampton in 2021.

checks.h: Delivering to a grain farm near harvest?
checks.p: Access on a cropping property is usually wide and firm. The catch is timing: at harvest the tracks are busy with trucks and headers, and so are you. Tell us when suits and where the container can go without being in the way.

checks.h: How close to the coast is it?
checks.p: Salt rides the wind right across town. Keep the paint in good order, rinse it now and then, and deal with scratches early. Cargo-worthy and new grades arrive sound; how long they stay that way comes down to upkeep.

checks.h: Will heat be a problem for what is inside?
checks.p: A Mid West summer makes the inside of a steel box very hot. Vents help and shade helps more. Keep heat-sensitive goods — chemicals, batteries, aerosols — out of it, or insulate it.

p: Anyone who has spent a summer in Geraldton knows the wind. The leaning trees on the Greenough flats grew that way for a reason. A container is heavy and sits well on the ground, but the doors, anything stacked beside it and anything loose on top are all at the wind's mercy.

Put the container where a building or a windbreak takes the brunt of the southerly. Keep the doors shut when you are not using them. Do not leave sheets of iron or timber leaning against it. Small habits, but in this town they count.

sections.h: Sand, limestone and the Greenough flats
p: Around the coastal suburbs the ground is sand over limestone — firm once compacted, and quick to drain. Out on the Greenough flats the soil is heavier alluvial ground that drains more slowly after rain, and in the Chapman Valley there are slopes and gravel to deal with.
Whatever the ground, set the container on solid pads at the corners, check it is level, and make sure water runs away from the doors rather than toward them.

sections.h: Dongara, Port Denison and the cray boats
p: South of Geraldton, Dongara and Port Denison are fishing towns as much as holiday towns, and the rock lobster fleet up and down this coast carries a lot of gear ashore between seasons: pots, ropes, floats, bait gear and spares. A container is a good place for it, with two caveats.

First, salt-soaked rope and pots bring the sea inside with them. Rinse and dry gear before it goes in, fit vents, and expect to wash the floor out now and then. Second, a container full of fishing gear gets heavy, so put it where a forklift or a ute can get right up to the doors. The same advice suits anybody storing boat gear in Geraldton itself — the steel lasts much longer when it is not wet with salt from the inside as well as the outside.

access: In town, a tilt-tray places most 10ft and 20ft units on an ordinary block. Tight frontages and backyards need a side loader or a crane. Beachside blocks at Drummond Cove and Cape Burney can be loose sand right up to the house, so tell us if the drive is unsealed.
Narngulu and the other industrial areas take 40ft units without fuss. On farms, a 40ft is fine if there is a firm track, wide gates and room to turn.
freight: Delivery is priced per job and included in the container quote. It depends on the run from Fremantle, where you are in the Mid West, and what the site needs. We do not publish a figure because the right one depends on your address.
locations.faqHead: Questions from Geraldton and the Mid West

faqs.q: Do you have a yard in Geraldton?
faqs.a: No. We have no office, yard or people in the Mid West. Stock for WA is held at a third-party depot in Fremantle, where you can inspect by arrangement, or we can send photos of the unit before delivery.

faqs.q: Will the wind move a container?
faqs.a: An empty 20ft is heavy, but strong wind still acts on it, and a container is not a rated structure. If it is staying long-term, ask the City of Greater Geraldton or an engineer what tie-down, if any, they expect. We do not supply any wind rating.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to a farm near Mullewa?
faqs.a: Yes. Tell us about the access, the gates and the track, and when suits you around seeding or harvest.

faqs.q: Is a cargo-worthy container watertight?
faqs.a: Cargo-worthy and new units are sold wind and watertight. As-is units are not sold watertight. For anything that must stay dry, do not go cheaper than cargo-worthy.

faqs.q: Do I need council approval?
faqs.a: It depends on your zoning, how long the container stays and what it is used for. Ask the City of Greater Geraldton — or the Shire of Chapman Valley, Irwin or Northampton if that is where you are.

faqs.q: Where will the doors face on delivery?
faqs.a: Wherever you tell us. On a tilt-tray the doors usually end up facing the truck's direction of travel or away from it, so think about the wind before the driver arrives and tell us which end you want where.

faqs.q: Can I hire one for a project inland?
faqs.a: Yes. Hire units are cargo-worthy or better. Tell us where the site is and roughly how long, and we will price hire against buying.

locations.askSub: Give us the address, the access and what it is for, and we will price the container with delivery from Fremantle.

locations.line: Kalgoorlie-Boulder is a long run east from the Fremantle depot where our Western Australian stock is held, out along the Great Eastern Highway. On the Goldfields the questions are about heat, red dust, mine-site rules and hard ground — so that is what this page answers.
locations.usesHead: What the Goldfields use containers for
uses: Mining drives Kalgoorlie-Boulder, and mining gets through a lot of containers: parts stores, tool rooms, core and sample storage, laydown boxes, and secure stores on exploration camps and contract sites. Contractors often need one on site for the life of a job and gone again afterwards, which makes hire a good fit.

In town, through Lamington, Somerville, South Kalgoorlie and out to Boulder, it is household storage, tradie stores and gear for people who come and go on rosters. On pastoral and prospecting blocks around the district, it is a secure lock-up for tools, detectors, camping gear and machinery parts on ground that is left empty for weeks at a time.
stock: We are not a Goldfields business and have no yard, office or staff in Kalgoorlie-Boulder. Our WA stock is held at a third-party depot in Fremantle, and a Kalgoorlie container travels the whole way out by road.

You can inspect the unit at the Fremantle depot by arrangement if you are in Perth, or ask for photos of the specific container on request, before delivery. On a run this long, knowing what is on the truck matters.
locations.checksIntro: Goldfields deliveries turn on paperwork and planning more than on the ground. Work through this list first.

checks.h: Mine or camp site: what are the entry rules?
checks.p: Mine sites and camps have inductions, drug and alcohol testing, vehicle requirements, radio protocols and set delivery windows. Send us the site's requirements and the name of whoever will meet the truck before we book. Some sites expect things of the vehicle or driver that we need to know about well in advance.

checks.h: Is the site on a sealed road?
checks.p: Plenty of Goldfields sites sit down a gravel or dirt road. Tell us the route from the highway, the state of the road, and whether recent rain has caused trouble. A big thunderstorm can close a dirt road for a while.

checks.h: Is the ground hard and level?
checks.p: Red clay, gravel and calcrete make firm ground across much of the district. Level the spot before the container arrives, or have packing ready for the corners. A container out of level twists, and the doors jam.

checks.h: What will the heat do to the contents?
checks.p: Summer on the Goldfields brings long runs of very hot days, and inside an uninsulated container it gets hotter again. Keep heat-sensitive goods — batteries, aerosols, chemicals, electronics — out of it, fit vents, and consider insulating it or shading it.

checks.h: Will dust get in?
checks.p: Fine red dust gets into everything. A cargo-worthy or new container has sound door seals and is sold wind and watertight, which keeps most of it out. Keep the seals clean and the doors shut when not in use.

checks.h: Older block in Boulder or Kalgoorlie?
checks.p: Many older blocks have a rear laneway. If yours does, tell us — a lane can be the easiest way in, or too narrow for a truck. Photos settle it.

p: Delivering a container to a mine or a contractor's yard is usually easy for the truck — flat ground, room to move, 40ft no problem. What can go wrong is the process: a driver not inducted, a purchase order not raised, a gatehouse not expecting the truck.

Get the site's requirements to us with the order, name a contact who will be there on the day, and mark where the container goes. If it will need moving to another part of the lease later, plan for that now.
The Goldfields swing from hot, dry summers to cold winter nights. Big temperature swings in a closed steel box cause condensation, even in a dry climate, and vents at both ends help a great deal.
The sun is hard on paint and rubber. Keep the container painted, keep dust from building up in the door channels, and check the seals now and then. A shaded spot makes the inside far more bearable.

sections.h: Roster life and a lock-up at home
p: Plenty of Kalgoorlie-Boulder households run on rosters, with the house empty or half-empty for stretches at a time. A container in the yard makes a better lock-up than a garden shed for tools, bikes, quads and camping gear while you are away, because there is no window to break and the doors are solid steel.

Get the most out of that by fitting a proper lock box over the padlock, placing the doors where they can be seen from the street or the house, and putting it on level ground so the doors seal well. If you are storing a quad or a generator, drain what you can first and think about ventilation — a closed box in the Goldfields heat is no place for fuel fumes to build up.

access: In town, most blocks are flat and easy for a tilt-tray placing a 10ft or 20ft. Check overhead wires and trees, and whether the approach is from the street or a laneway. If it is a lane, measure it at its narrowest and look for power poles, bins and fences leaning into it.
Industrial yards and mine sites usually take a 40ft without trouble. Remote sites need a firm road the whole way in and space for the truck to turn.
locations.freightHead: The cost of the trip east
freight: Getting a container to the Goldfields is a long haul, and the cost depends on the run, the truck the site needs and any requirements at the other end. We quote it with the container for your address. A number printed here would be wrong for most sites.

faqs.q: Do you have a yard in Kalgoorlie?
faqs.a: No. We have no premises on the Goldfields. WA stock is held at a third-party depot in Fremantle; you can inspect a unit there by arrangement, or we send photographs before delivery.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to a mine site?
faqs.a: Yes, subject to the site's requirements. Send them with the order along with a site contact. If the site needs anything particular from the driver or truck, we need to know before we book.

faqs.q: Should I hire or buy for a contract?
faqs.a: For a contract with an end date, hire is often simpler. For a permanent store, buying usually works out better. We will price both.

faqs.q: How hot does it get inside?
faqs.a: Very hot in summer. Fine for tools and hardware; not for batteries, chemicals, electronics or food. Vents, shade and insulation make a big difference.

faqs.q: Do I need approval from the City of Kalgoorlie-Boulder?
faqs.a: It depends on the zoning, how long the container stays and what it is for. On a mining lease, the tenement holder's rules apply as well. Check before delivery.

faqs.q: Can I see photos before it is sent?
faqs.a: Yes. Ask for photos of the actual unit and we will send them on request, before delivery. With a run this long, it is worth looking at the floor, the doors and the seals in those photos before the truck leaves Fremantle.

faqs.q: Can it go out to a prospecting block?
faqs.a: Yes, if the road in will carry a truck. Tell us the route and the road condition. After a storm, dirt roads may need time to dry out.
